articles.title: CHERI Capability Machines vs MMU Virtual Memory: Two Ideas of a Pointer
articles.excerpt: Most memory corruption bugs come from a simple fact: in a conventional computer, a pointer is just an integer. If a program computes the wrong address, the hardware has no way to know the mistake is a…
articles.body: Most memory corruption bugs come from a simple fact: in a conventional computer, a pointer is just an integer. If a program computes the wrong address, the hardware has no way to know the mistake is a mistake — it happily reads or writes whatever the number says. The memory management unit, or MMU, was the twentieth century's answer, dividing memory into pages and checking access at page granularity. CHERI, a capability-machine architecture developed over more than a decade, proposes a different answer: make every pointer a hardware-protected token that carries its own bounds and permissions. The two approaches protect the same memory but disagree fundamentally about what a reference to memory should be.

articles.title: RAG Not Finding Answers? Five Knowledge Base Problems
articles.excerpt: This is the most common failure after a RAG knowledge base goes live, and the hardest to track down, because it throws no error. The upload shows success, the admin panel is green, and the chat still…
articles.body: This is the most common failure after a RAG knowledge base goes live, and the hardest to track down, because it throws no error . The upload shows success, the admin panel is green, and the chat still cannot find the answer. Below are five causes we traced on production systems, ordered from the outside in. 1. The disk filled up and the vector store went read-only This is the outermost cause and the one people skip. Something else on the machine fills the disk, the vector database switches itself to read-only, and new content never gets written. The upload screen still says success. The symptom: old content is found, nothing added this week is. Check the disk level before anything else. It saves hours. On a self-hosted setup, set a disk alert at 80%, before this happens, not after. 2.

articles.title: JIT vs AOT Compilation: Startup Pain Versus Peak Speed
articles.excerpt: Every program must eventually become machine code, but the moment that translation happens changes almost everything about how the program behaves. Ahead-of-time compilation, or AOT, turns source into…
articles.body: Every program must eventually become machine code, but the moment that translation happens changes almost everything about how the program behaves. Ahead-of-time compilation, or AOT, turns source into a native binary before the program is ever launched, the way a C or Rust toolchain does. Just-in-time compilation, or JIT, leaves source or bytecode in a portable form and compiles it during execution, the way the Java Virtual Machine and JavaScript engines do. Neither is simply faster. They optimise for different points on a timeline: one pays its cost before you press enter, the other pays it while you are already waiting.

articles.title: SMR vs CMR Hard Drives: The Capacity Trick That Costs You Latency
articles.excerpt: A hard drive platter is a finite piece of glass, and the industry has been squeezing more bits onto it for decades. Conventional magnetic recording, or CMR, writes each track independently with a smal…
articles.body: A hard drive platter is a finite piece of glass, and the industry has been squeezing more bits onto it for decades. Conventional magnetic recording, or CMR, writes each track independently with a small guard gap between them. Shingled magnetic recording, or SMR, overlaps tracks like roof shingles so that one track's edge sits partly on top of its neighbour, reclaiming the guard gap and packing significantly more data into the same physical area. The catch is that you can no longer overwrite a single track in place without damaging the one next to it. That one mechanical fact explains almost every performance difference between the two.

articles.title: If Your AI Feature Loses Internet Access, What Can Users Still Do?
articles.excerpt: You’re editing a document with an AI writing tool. You highlight a paragraph, ask for a rewrite, and keep typing while it works. Then the connection drops. When it comes back, the original paragraph i…
articles.body: You’re editing a document with an AI writing tool. You highlight a paragraph, ask for a rewrite, and keep typing while it works. Then the connection drops. When it comes back, the original paragraph is still there, but the status just says Something went wrong . Now you have three questions. Were your latest edits saved? Is the rewrite still coming? Can you keep working without it? Those are product questions. The answers depend on what your app does when it loses its connection to the model. Keep the user’s work available In a writing app, the document and the AI suggestion have different jobs. The document holds the user’s work. The suggestion is a proposed change they can accept or ignore. Design the failure around that difference.

articles.title: Building Uptime Monitoring
articles.excerpt: Introduction to Uptime Monitoring I built SitePulse to help freelancers and small agencies monitor their clients' websites. One of the main challenges they face is ensuring their clients' sites are al…
articles.body: Introduction to Uptime Monitoring I built SitePulse to help freelancers and small agencies monitor their clients' websites. One of the main challenges they face is ensuring their clients' sites are always available. This can be a daunting task, especially when dealing with multiple sites. Handling Uptime Checks SitePulse checks for uptime by sending requests to the site and expecting an answer within 10 seconds. If the site doesn't respond or returns an error status twice in a row, and checks from both Europe and Asia can't reach it, the site is considered down. However, if either region can still reach the site, no alert is sent. I also implemented 'page must contain' checks, which allow users to specify text that must be present on the page for it to be considered up.

articles.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
articles.excerpt: Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.
articles.body: For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth.

articles.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
articles.excerpt: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.
articles.body: The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it.

articles.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.
articles.body: A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.
